svg.title: The four layers that protect data, and what slips past each one
svg.desc: A write travels downward through four defences: application validation, the schema's constraints, the transaction boundary, and the durable file with its backup. Each layer lists what it catches and what gets past it. Only the schema layer applies to every writer.
svg.text: Four layers stand between a bad value and a permanently wrong row
Read down the middle. The green line is what each layer stops; the red line is what walks straight through it.
a write arrives
INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE
1 · Application validation
your Python, your web form, your loader script
catches: typos, empty fields, a friendly message before anything is attempted
slips past: every writer that is not this program — a console session, a colleague's script, a second service, a bug in the validator itself
2 · The schema's constraints
NOT NULL · UNIQUE · CHECK · DEFAULT · PRIMARY KEY · FOREIGN KEY · STRICT
catches: the same mistakes, from EVERY writer, forever — including the one-off script nobody reviewed
slips past: rules needing more than one row at a time; CHECK may not contain a subquery
slips past: foreign keys entirely, unless PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON is set on this connection
This is the layer that wins ties. It is the only one that is still enforced at three in the morning.
3 · The transaction boundary
BEGIN … COMMIT, or BEGIN … ROLLBACK
catches: a multi-statement change that must not half-happen; a change you look at and decide against
slips past: a statement error does NOT roll the transaction back — COMMIT after an error keeps what already succeeded
slips past: a WHERE-less UPDATE you then commit. It was never invalid, only wrong.
4 · The durable file, and the copy you took first
slips past: nothing. There is no layer after this one, which is why the copy is not optional.
Validation is a courtesy to the user. A constraint is a promise to everyone who will ever write to this table.
